note: A tomb messenger announces resurrection and Galilee. Matthew also depicts Jesus meeting the women.
A tomb announcement to women. Luke recalls a prediction made in Galilee and narrates their report to the others.
Women receive a resurrection announcement. Luke gives the messengers a different reminder and has no encounter with Jesus in this scene.
Peter inspects the tomb and linen. John includes a second disciple and distinguishes their reactions.
Jesus gives women a message for others. Matthew names Galilee as the destination. John gives Mary a message about ascent.
A commission involving the nations. Matthew specifies baptism and instruction, Luke repentance and forgiveness beginning in Jerusalem.
The risen Jesus sends disciples. John frames sending through the Father, the Spirit and forgiveness.
Both commission a wide mission. Mark’s disputed longer ending connects belief, baptism and signs.
Jesus appears among gathered followers with a greeting of peace and shows wounds. Luke adds the meal and scriptural exposition. John adds the breathing of the Spirit.
Jesus greets the group with peace on two occasions in the same Gospel. Thomas is present only on the second occasion.
Both commission the Twelve and regulate travel and lodging. Mark permits a staff, whereas Luke's packing instruction prohibits one.
Herod hears competing identities. Mark narrates John's execution at length; Luke gives Herod a question about the man he now hears of.
Returning apostles, a command to feed the crowd, five loaves and two fish. Luke specifies groups of about fifty, while Mark reports groups of hundreds and fifties.
Questions about identity precede Peter's confession and a prediction of suffering. Luke frames the exchange with prayer and omits the rebuke of Peter here.
Peter identifies Jesus in both. Matthew adds the blessing and keys. The suffering prediction belongs to Matthew's next unit.
Both ask about public opinion before Peter's confession. Matthew addresses Peter with promises, Luke moves to silence and suffering.
Both narrate the prediction and Peter's objection. Matthew's parent also contains the ensuing address on discipleship.
Both link losing life with taking up the cross. Mark explicitly gathers the crowd with disciples; Matthew introduces this teaching as an address to disciples.
Both move from renunciation to losing life and the Son of Man's response. Luke includes the kingdom promise within this indexed unit.
Both recount the mountain appearance, Peter and the heavenly voice. Luke identifies the subject of the conversation with Moses and Elijah, while Mark includes a descent discussion.
A father asks for help after the disciples' failure. Mark develops the father's exchange about belief and a private question afterward.
Both place a betrayal prediction beside the disciples' incomprehension. Mark explicitly adds killing and rising in this saying.
A dispute about greatness leads to receiving a child. Mark places the child among the Twelve and Luke beside Jesus.
John reports stopping an outsider and Jesus objects. Mark extends the response to a cup of water.
A sign is requested and refused. Matthew's response makes an exception for Jonah and then shifts to the disciples.
Leaven is misunderstood as bread. Mark names Herod, Matthew the Sadducees. Matthew explicitly narrates the disciples' eventual understanding.
Both debate divorce through Moses and creation. Matthew includes an exception and eunuch sayings. Mark gives a two-sided remarriage ruling in private.
Luke's compact remarriage saying lacks the dispute and private explanation that frame Mark's ruling.
The remarriage prohibition overlaps. Luke supplies neither Matthew's explicit exception nor its debate about celibacy here.
Children are brought, disciples object and Jesus welcomes them. Mark adds a saying about receiving the kingdom like a child.
A wealthy inquirer and instruction about wealth lead to discussion with disciples. Matthew includes thrones and judging Israel in the reply to Peter.
Both depict disruption of temple commerce. John places the episode early and adds the temple-body exchange. Mark surrounds the action with the fig tree and cites the house of prayer.
Both report a saying about a prophet's honor. John recalls it while describing a return to Galilee. Mark gives it as Jesus' response to offense in his hometown.
Five loaves, two fish and twelve baskets appear in both. John names Philip and Andrew, introduces a boy and narrates an attempt to make Jesus king.
Both recount the water crossing after the feeding and Jesus' reassurance. Mark emphasizes wind and the disciples' misunderstanding. John ends with the boat reaching its destination.

Both introduce Simon and Andrew as followers. John begins with the Baptist's testimony and Andrew bringing Simon. Mark gives a shoreside call to fishermen. The sequence and initiating speakers differ.
A costly anointing and an objection about the poor. John names Mary and Judas and describes feet and hair. Mark describes an unnamed woman anointing the head.
Entry and acclamation overlap. Mark narrates instructions to obtain a colt. John describes Jesus finding a young donkey and the disciples remembering afterward.
Both predict Peter's denials. In John the exchange follows Peter's question about following Jesus. Mark places it after a prediction of wider desertion on the way to the Mount of Olives.
Arrest and the injury to a servant overlap. John names Peter and Malchus and reports the exchange about the cup. Mark narrates a kiss and leaves the armed individual unnamed.
Pilate questions Jesus about kingship. John develops the origin of the kingdom and testimony to truth. Mark emphasizes the brief response and silence under accusation.
Both narrate the death and sour wine. The recorded final words and the witnesses emphasized in the narratives differ.
Joseph obtains the body. John includes Nicodemus and spices. Mark reports Pilate checking the death and women observing the burial place.
Both report baptism and the heavenly voice. Matthew records an exchange about righteousness and gives the voice in the third person.
The wilderness testing follows baptism in each account. Mark gives no dialogue or sequence of three tests.
Both connect the arrest of John to proclamation in Galilee. Mark includes a call to believe the good news. Matthew sets the move to Capernaum alongside Isaiah.
The same two pairs of brothers are called by the lake. Mark also mentions hired workers left with Zebedee.
Only the divorce saying in Matthew 5:31–32 is compared. Luke places his saying in a different discourse and gives no explicit exception.
Both invoke a lamp placed on a stand. Matthew applies it to visible good works, while Mark connects it to disclosure and hearing.
A request for cleansing, touch and priestly presentation occur in both. Mark adds the effect of publicity on where Jesus can enter.
Lodging and burial replies recur. Luke sets them on the journey and adds an encounter about farewell and the plow.
In Matthew Jesus challenges the disciples before addressing the storm. Mark places the questions about fear and faith after it becomes calm.
Both have demons, pigs and a request for Jesus to leave. Matthew narrates two men, while Mark concentrates on one and adds a commission to report what happened.
Both connect a healing command with authority to forgive. Mark narrates opening a roof and lowering the man.
The tax booth call leads to a meal and a physician saying. Matthew names Matthew and adds the Hosea citation; Mark names Levi.
Both answer the fasting question with bridegroom, cloth and wine images. Matthew presents the question explicitly from John’s disciples.
Both interweave two healings. Matthew introduces the girl as already dead and omits the words that Mark addresses to her.
Shared instructions concern travel, lodging and rejection. Mark permits a staff and directs the travelers to wear sandals. Matthew places staff and sandals in the list of things not to acquire.
The Twelve receive a healing and proclamation mission with directions about lodging. Matthew adds the Israel-only destination and an explicit comparison with Sodom and Gomorrah.
The grain dispute invokes David in both. Matthew adds priestly temple service and a mercy citation, then moves to another Sabbath dispute.
Compare Matthew 12:9–14 specifically. Both heal a withered hand. Matthew includes the rescue of a sheep.
Both answer an allegation about demonic power with a divided kingdom and strong man. Matthew continues to fruit and accountability for words.
Both recast family through doing God's will. Matthew explicitly gestures toward the disciples.
Compare the sower story before the crowd. Mark's indexed parent also contains the explanation given afterward.
Compare the private question and interpretation. Matthew expands the scriptural citation and blesses the disciples' eyes and ears.
Both compare the kingdom to a mustard seed and describe parabolic teaching. Matthew also gives the leaven comparison and a fulfillment citation.
Both report offense and a proverb about a prophet's hometown. Mark calls Jesus a carpenter, while Matthew's townspeople call him the carpenter's son.
Herod interprets Jesus through John's death. Mark supplies a longer account of the banquet and describes Herod's attitude toward John.
Both feed five thousand from five loaves and two fish. Mark relates the scene to the apostles' return and the teaching of the crowd.
The sea crossing and reassurance overlap. Matthew adds Peter's attempt and the confession in the boat.
Both name Gennesaret and associate healing with the garment's fringe. Mark follows the movement into multiple settlements.
Both move from handwashing and provision for parents to defilement. Matthew closes by expressly returning to eating with unwashed hands.
Both include the exchange over children's food. Matthew calls the woman Canaanite and adds the explicit lost-sheep saying.
Both recount seven loaves, four thousand and seven baskets. Matthew explicitly mentions women and children beyond the men counted.
Both present the mountain scene and Elijah discussion. Matthew records Jesus touching the frightened disciples and telling them to rise.
Both connect a boy's healing to disciples' inability. Mark expands the conversation with the father and sets the private explanation in a house.
Both record a prediction in Galilee. Matthew describes grief, while Mark reports incomprehension and fear of asking.
Both specify Jerusalem, handing over and Gentile mistreatment. Matthew expressly names crucifixion.
Both use the cup, status reversal and service. Matthew introduces the request through the mother while Mark gives it to the sons.
Matthew depicts two men outside Jericho. Mark identifies Bartimaeus and gives an exchange with a single petitioner.
Both describe securing an animal and the entry acclamation. Matthew specifies a donkey and colt and adds a fulfillment citation.
Both develop the fig tree incident into teaching on prayer. Matthew has immediate withering. Mark depicts discovery the following morning.
In each temple exchange a question about authority leads to a counterquestion about John's baptism and deliberation by the leaders.
Both include tenants, a murdered son and a rejected stone. Matthew has the listeners voice the vineyard owner's verdict.
Both depict a test using a tax coin, the image and inscription, and an answer distinguishing what belongs to Caesar and God.
Both answer the Sadducees' seven-brothers case through resurrection and the patriarchs. Matthew ends with a reaction from the crowd.
Both join love of God and neighbor. Mark adds the scribe's favorable reply and Jesus' comment about proximity to the kingdom.
Both ask how David's lord can be his son. Matthew stages the opening as a question and answer with the Pharisees.
Both alternate prayer and sleeping disciples. Matthew supplies wording for a second prayer before reporting the third.
Compare the hearing within Mark's broader arrest passage. Both distinguish testimony about the temple from Jesus' own answer to the high priest.
Both narrate Peter's denials and recollection. Matthew names one crowing in the remembered saying; Mark's wording counts two.
Both report the cry of abandonment and the misunderstanding about Elijah. Matthew adds an earthquake and opened tombs.
Both connect Jesus, his Father and the temple. Luke narrates a childhood exchange with parents and John a public confrontation in adulthood.
Both include a descent and heavenly declaration. Luke emphasizes prayer and omits Matthew's dialogue between Jesus and John.
Both narrate three temptations with scripture on the lips of Jesus and the devil. Their second and third settings occur in reverse order.
Hometown rejection and a prophetic proverb overlap. Luke adds the Isaiah reading, Elijah and Elisha examples and attempted violence.
Fishermen leave to follow in both. Luke places a catch and Simon's exchange with Jesus before the departure.
Both use bridegroom, cloth and wine in response to a fasting question. Luke gives the further saying about preferring old wine.
Blessings for poverty, hunger and persecution overlap. Luke uses direct address and pairs blessings with woes. Matthew qualifies poverty and hunger differently.
Both include enemy love and resistance to reciprocity. Compare Matthew 5:38–48 in particular. Luke concludes with the Father's mercy and explicitly discusses lending.
Both join judgment and the speck-and-beam illustration. Luke also speaks of giving and blind guides, while Matthew includes dogs and pearls.
Both finish a discourse with two builders and the need to act on Jesus' words. Luke describes digging deep and a swollen river.
The authority analogy and praise of a centurion's faith overlap. Luke uses elders and friends as intermediaries, while Matthew stages direct speech.
John's messengers receive an answer through a list of signs and a blessing. Luke narrates healings at the time of the inquiry.
Anointing at a meal attracts objections. Luke focuses on hospitality, debt and forgiveness, while Mark frames the act in relation to burial. The women are not identified as the same person.
Both include the name Legion and a commission to the healed man. Luke explicitly reports his request to accompany Jesus before the direction to return home.
Travel, greetings, food and rejected towns overlap. Luke addresses an additional group after the Twelve's mission. Matthew specifies the Twelve and an Israel-only destination.
Thanksgiving and sayings about Father and Son overlap. Luke moves to a private blessing of the disciples. Matthew continues with rest for the burdened.
Compare Luke 11:2–4 and Matthew 6:9–13. Luke situates the prayer in a response to a disciple and follows it with the midnight request. Matthew situates it within the sermon.
Jonah, Nineveh and the Queen of the South recur. Matthew explicitly compares Jonah's three days with the Son of Man's time in the earth.
Birds and flowers illustrate care and the limits of anxiety. Luke continues directly to selling possessions and giving alms.
Refused invitations lead to a widened guest list. Matthew depicts a royal wedding, violence and the guest without a wedding garment. Luke develops specific excuses and the host's further invitations.
Both use a straying sheep. Luke replies to complaints about receiving sinners and emphasizes repentance. Matthew addresses the treatment of little ones.
Both use entrusted money and returning authority. Luke adds opponents of a nobleman's kingship. Matthew distinguishes the initial sums entrusted.
Both instruct flight from Judea and anticipate distress. Luke identifies surrounding armies and captivity; Matthew refers to the desolating sacrilege.
Bread and cup sayings overlap. Luke describes a cup before the bread as well as a cup afterward in the longer textual form.
Both describe arrest and injury by sword. Luke reports healing the ear. Matthew gives the longer rebuke about the sword and angelic aid.
Both include darkness, Jesus' death and a centurion's response. Luke gives a prayer of entrusting the spirit and a different declaration by the centurion.
